patient_information: A 24-year-old woman from the highlands of Peru is transferred to a hospital in the capital, Lima. Prior to her current illness, she was healthy. She is single and has no children.
chief_complaint: 2-month history of upper abdominal pain, weight loss (5 kg), nausea and vomiting, and intermittent fevers for the past 2 weeks.
history_of_present_illness: A 24-year-old woman presented with a 2-month history of upper abdominal pain, weight loss (5 kg), nausea and vomiting. She tried analgesics, which did not control the pain. She also reports intermittent fevers for the past 2 weeks. Three days previously, she was seen at the emergency room for these complaints, where abdominal ultrasound revealed multiple hypoechoic lesions in her liver. She was treated with ceftriaxone and metronidazole for suspected pyogenic liver abscesses but did not show any clinical improvement.
exposure_and_epidemiology: The patient is from the highlands of Peru. About 2 to 3 months ago she started taking over-the-counter medicines to lose weight and changed her diet to vegetarian food. She also reported the consumption of energetic hot drinks made from alfalfa and watercress.
vitals: Her blood pressure is 95/60mmHg, pulse 105 bpm and temperature 38.5°C (101.3°F).
physical_exam: The patient looks ill, with pale mucous membranes but no jaundice. On palpation of the abdomen there is right upper quadrant tenderness, and the liver is slightly enlarged with a liver span of 15 cm. The rest of the physical examination is normal.
labs_and_diagnostics: Abdominal ultrasound revealed multiple hypoechoic lesions in her liver. A contrast-enhanced CT scan of her abdomen shows multiple hypodense, non-enhancing lesions in the liver (Fig. 67.1). Laboratory results on admission included WBC 13.94 (x 10^9/L), Eosinophils 43% (<5 reference range), Total eosinophil count 5.97 (<0.5 reference range), Haemoglobin 12.3 g/dL (12-16 reference range), AST 34 U/L (10-40 reference range), ALT 55 U/L (7-40 reference range), AP 170 U/L (20-126 reference range), Amylase 75 U/L (3-100 reference range), and Lipase 100 U/L (10-140 reference range). The Fas2 ELISA titre was 0.56 (normal <0.2).
differential_diagnosis: Initial differential diagnosis included suspected pyogenic liver abscesses, but the lack of improvement after 3 days of appropriate antibiotic treatment made this diagnosis less likely. Given the patient's origin from the Andes, high eosinophilia, and history of alfalfa and watercress consumption, fascioliasis was considered the most important diagnosis. Amoebic liver abscess was also considered, but eosinophilia and multiple lesions are not typical, and it's uncommon in young women and should respond to metronidazole. Other endemic infections in Peru included brucellosis, visceral toxocariasis, or secondary infections with ascariasis and hydatid disease. Opisthorchis was considered if there was travel history to South-east Asia.
management_and_clinical_course: Initially, she was treated with ceftriaxone and metronidazole, which did not show clinical improvement. After the Fas2 ELISA confirmed the diagnosis of fascioliasis, the patient received one single dose of triclabendazole 10 mg/kg. Her clinical symptoms rapidly improved, and her laboratory parameters went back to normal. On control tomography, her liver lesions were seen to be disappearing.
final_diagnosis: The final diagnosis was fascioliasis, caused by the liver fluke Fasciola hepatica. This was supported by the patient's history of fever, weight loss, abdominal pain, consumption of watercress, pronounced eosinophilia, and multiple hypodense non-enhancing hepatic lesions on CT scan. The diagnosis was confirmed by a Fas2 ELISA titre of 0.56 (normal <0.2), and the patient showed rapid clinical improvement and resolution of liver lesions after a single dose of triclabendazole.
